title: Gramática clínica: Grammar for Patient Care
summary: Master the core grammar patients and clinicians use to describe health and feelings.

lessons.title: Ser vs. Estar: Identity vs. Condition

levels.kid:
Spanish has two words that both mean "to be." They are **ser** and **estar**. That sounds tricky, but here is a trick.

Think of **ser** like a name tag. It tells who or what you are, and that stays with you. "Soy Odin" means "I am Odin." "Soy doctor" means "I am a doctor."

Think of **estar** like a weather report. It tells how you are right now, or where you are. "Estoy cansado" means "I am tired." Later you can rest and feel better! "Estoy en el hospital" means "I am in the hospital."

Doctors use both. "Soy la doctora" means "I am the doctor." "¿Cómo está?" means "How are you feeling?"
levels.hs:
Spanish splits English "to be" into two verbs. Choosing the right one matters a lot in a clinic.

**Ser** describes identity and defining traits: who someone is, what they are, where they are from, and what time it is.
- Soy el doctor Ruiz. (I am Dr. Ruiz.)
- Es diabético. (He is diabetic. This is a lasting condition.)
- Son las tres. (It is three o'clock.)

**Estar** describes states and conditions that can change, and location.
- Estoy enfermo. (I am sick.)
- Está mareada. (She is dizzy.)
- El baño está a la derecha. (The bathroom is on the right.)

Present-tense forms:
- ser: soy, eres, es, somos, son
- estar: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están

In medical Spanish you will mostly use the formal **usted** form, which shares the él/ella form: "¿Está usted cansado?" (Are you tired?).

A useful memory aid is **DOCTOR** for ser: Description, Occupation, Characteristic, Time, Origin, Relationship. For estar, use **PLACE**: Position, Location, Action, Condition, Emotion.

A real example: a nurse asks "¿Cómo está?" (How are you feeling today?), not "¿Cómo es?", which would mean "What are you like as a person?"
levels.college:
The ser/estar contrast is less about permanent versus temporary and more about **essence versus state**. Ser classifies or defines something. Estar reports a condition or a location relative to some moment.

**Core uses of ser**
- Identity and profession: Soy enfermera. Note that no article is used before an unmodified profession.
- Inherent traits and diagnoses treated as categories: Es alérgico a la penicilina. Es hipertenso.
- Origin and nationality: Es de Guatemala.
- Time, dates and events: La cita es a las diez. La cirugía es en el quirófano 3. Here the location of an event takes ser.
- Passive voice: Fue operado ayer (He was operated on yesterday).

**Core uses of estar**
- Physical and emotional states: Está pálido, débil, nervioso, deprimida.
- Location of people and things: El paciente está en la UCI.
- Progressive tenses: Está sangrando (He is bleeding). ¿Está tomando algún medicamento?
- Results of a process: La herida está cerrada. Está embarazada.

**Exceptions that trip learners**
- Death takes estar even though it is permanent: Está muerto. Here the state results from an event.
- Many adjectives change meaning with the verb:
- ser malo (bad), estar malo (ill)
- ser listo (clever), estar listo (ready)
- ser aburrido (boring), estar aburrido (bored)
- ser vivo (sharp, lively), estar vivo (alive)

Clinically, "¿Está bien?" checks how the patient feels now. Saying "Es nervioso" labels the patient as a nervous person. "Está nervioso" means he is anxious right now, which is usually what you mean at the bedside.
levels.phd:
Linguists frame the contrast through the distinction between **individual-level** and **stage-level** predication (Carlson, 1977). Ser goes with individual-level predicates, which characterize an entity across situations. Estar goes with stage-level predicates, which hold of a temporally bounded stage. Some analyses go further. Maienborn argues that estar presupposes a link to a specific discourse situation. Others treat estar as aspectual, marking a predicate as the outcome of a change or comparison. Both views explain why "Está muerto" uses estar. Death is permanent, but the predicate describes a resultant state tied to an event.

This framework predicts subtle clinical contrasts:
- "Es diabético" classifies the patient within a category. "Está diabético" is nonstandard in most varieties.
- "El niño es delgado" describes his build. "El niño está delgado" implies he looks thin compared with a norm or with before. That comparative reading can flag weight loss.
- "Está muy alto" (he has gotten so tall) contrasts with his past self. "Es alto" is a stable description.

These comparative readings explain why native speakers say "¡Qué guapa estás!" for how someone looks today.

There is also **regional variation**. In Mexican and some Central American Spanish, estar has expanded into contexts that Peninsular Spanish reserves for ser, such as "Está muy grande la clínica." Silva-Corvalán documented that the expansion of estar is faster in U.S. bilingual communities, likely under contact pressure. Clinicians serving these communities will hear estar used more broadly.

Location splits by referent type. Entities take estar: "El laboratorio está en el segundo piso." Events take ser, meaning "take place": "La reunión es en la sala 4." The test is whether the verb can be paraphrased as "tener lugar."

Acquisition research shows that English-speaking learners overextend ser early on and learn estar plus adjective late. This is why instructors drill symptom adjectives with estar.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, ser/estar errors are rarely fatal. They can, however, distort the clinical record, stigmatize patients, or cause confusion. High-yield contrasts for clinicians:

- **Labeling versus describing.** "Es alcohólico" defines a person by a disorder. Person-first phrasing such as "Tiene un trastorno por consumo de alcohol" is preferred in modern notes and conversation. Likewise, "Es epiléptico" is increasingly replaced by "Tiene epilepsia."
- **Mental status.** "Está confundido" or "Está desorientado" documents an acute finding and suggests delirium. "Es confuso" means that something, such as an explanation, is unclear. Mixing these up in a neuro exam handoff changes the meaning.
- **Consciousness.** "¿Está despierto?" (Is he awake?) differs from "Es despierto" (He is sharp or alert by nature). Use estar for level of consciousness: está somnoliento, está inconsciente.
- **Readiness and outcome.** "Ya está listo para la cirugía" means prepared. "Es listo" means clever. "Está grave" means critically ill. "Es grave" refers to the seriousness of a problem: "La lesión es grave."
- **Pregnancy.** Use "está embarazada." Avoid the false cognate "embarazada" for embarrassed. The correct phrase is "tiene vergüenza" or "está avergonzado."

Pitfalls in survey and screening instruments: translated questionnaires sometimes render "Are you depressed?" as "¿Es usted deprimido?" This is ungrammatical and implies a trait. Validated versions use "¿Se ha sentido deprimido?" or "¿Está deprimido?"

For neurosurgery-bound learners, family updates rely on estar. Examples: "Está estable," "Está en recuperación," "Está sedado pero responde." Ser frames the facts of the procedure: "La operación es mañana," "El tumor es benigno." The pathology finding is a classification, so it takes ser even if surgery later removes the tumor.

Open issues: dialect-driven expansion of estar means that nonstandard uses heard from patients are not errors to correct. Certified interpreters should be used for consent. Grammar competence does not replace qualified interpretation.

keyPoints: Ser = identity, traits, origin, time, events; estar = states, conditions, location
Ser forms: soy, eres, es, somos, son; estar: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están
Ask ¿Cómo está? to check how a patient feels right now
Death and pregnancy take estar: está muerto, está embarazada
Meaning shifts: ser malo (bad) vs estar malo (ill); ser listo vs estar listo
Event location takes ser: La cirugía es en el quirófano 3

test.q: Which sentence correctly says 'She is dizzy'?
test.explain: Dizziness is a current condition, so it takes estar. 'Es mareada' would wrongly present it as a trait.

test.q: To introduce yourself as the nurse, you say:
test.explain: Occupation is identity, so it takes ser. No article is used before an unmodified profession.

test.q: 'The patient is in the ICU' in Spanish is:
choices: El paciente soy en la UCI.
El paciente es en la UCI.
El paciente son en la UCI.
El paciente está en la UCI.
test.explain: The location of a person or thing takes estar.

test.q: Why does 'La cirugía es en el quirófano 3' use ser?
choices: The subject is an event taking place
Ser marks the location of objects
test.explain: The location of an event, meaning 'takes place,' uses ser. People and objects take estar.

test.q: What does 'Está malo' mean?
test.explain: Estar malo means to be ill. Ser malo means to be bad.

test.q: Which phrase asks how a patient is feeling today?
test.explain: ¿Cómo está? asks about a current state. ¿Cómo es? asks what someone is like as a person.

test.q: Death is permanent, yet 'He is dead' is:
test.explain: Muerto takes estar because it is a resultant state, which shows that 'permanent vs temporary' is only a rough rule.

test.q: 'Es alérgico a la penicilina' uses ser because the allergy is:
test.explain: Lasting conditions treated as categories, like allergies or diabetes, take ser.

test.q: 'Está sangrando' (He is bleeding) uses estar because it is:
test.explain: Progressive tenses (estar + -ndo) describe actions in progress, such as an ongoing action like bleeding.

test.q: The present-tense 'yo' form of estar is ___.
test.explain: Estar is conjugated estoy, estás, está, estamos, están.

test.q: Which verb would you use with 'embarazada' (pregnant)?
test.explain: Pregnancy is a state, so we say 'está embarazada.'

test.q: The ser memory aid DOCTOR stands for Description, Occupation, Characteristic, Time, Origin and ___.
test.explain: Relationships, such as 'Es mi hermano,' take ser.

kidTest.q: Which verb is like a name tag that tells who you are?
kidTest.explain: Ser tells who or what you are, as in 'Soy Odin.'

kidTest.q: What does 'Estoy cansado' mean?
kidTest.explain: Tired is how you feel right now, so it uses estar.

kidTest.q: Estar is like which of these?
choices: A name tag on your shirt
kidTest.explain: Estar tells how you are right now or where you are, and that can change, like a daily weather report.

kidTest.q: How does a doctor ask 'How are you feeling?'
kidTest.explain: ¿Cómo está? asks how someone feels now.

kidTest.q: Fill in: '___ Odin' means 'I am Odin.' (hint: s _ _)
kidTest.explain: Soy is the 'I' form of ser.

advancedTest.q: A parent says 'El niño está delgado.' The best clinical reading is:
choices: The child has an inherited thin body type
The child looks thin compared with a norm or before
The child has a naturally slim build
The sentence is ungrammatical in standard Spanish
advancedTest.explain: Estar with a size adjective has a comparative, stage-level reading that can flag weight loss. A stable build would use ser.

advancedTest.q: Under the stage-level analysis, 'Está muerto' uses estar because:
choices: It marks a state resulting from an event
Spanish uses estar for inborn physical traits
Death is viewed as a temporary condition
Muerto is classed as a location word in Spanish
advancedTest.explain: Estar marks a state resulting from a change, not temporariness, which is why permanence does not force ser.

advancedTest.q: A Mexican-American patient says 'Está muy grande la clínica.' The clinician should:
choices: Correct it because ser is required here
Ask an interpreter to report a speech disorder
Recognize regional expansion of estar as normal usage
Assume the clinic has recently gotten bigger
advancedTest.explain: Estar has expanded into ser contexts in Mexican and U.S. contact varieties. This is dialect variation, not error.

advancedTest.q: Why is 'Está confundido' preferred to 'Es confuso' in a neuro handoff?
choices: Both phrases convey the same mental-status finding
Es confuso is the more formal written version
Estar reports an acute finding; es confuso means unclear
Confundido takes ser in most medical charts
advancedTest.explain: Está confundido documents an acute change that may suggest delirium. Es confuso describes something, such as an explanation, as unclear.

lessons.title: Present Tense of Regular -ar, -er and -ir Verbs

levels.kid:
In Spanish, action words are called **verbs**. Each verb has an ending that tells you its family: **-ar**, **-er** or **-ir**.

Think of a verb like a train. The front part stays the same. The last car changes depending on who is doing the action.

- **hablar** = to talk. **Yo hablo** = I talk.
- **comer** = to eat. **Yo como** = I eat.
- **vivir** = to live. **Yo vivo** = I live.

See? For "I," you take off the family ending and add **-o**.

Doctors use verbs all the time. A doctor might ask, "¿Usted come bien?" That means "Do you eat well?" With just a few verb endings, you can ask many kind questions.
levels.hs:
A **verb** shows an action or a state. In Spanish, the basic form is the **infinitive**, which ends in **-ar**, **-er** or **-ir** (hablar, comer, vivir). To use a verb in the **present tense**, drop the ending to find the **stem**, then add an ending that matches the subject. Changing the ending like this is called **conjugation**.

**-ar verbs (hablar, to speak):** hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan

**-er verbs (comer, to eat):** como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen

**-ir verbs (vivir, to live):** vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven

The -er and -ir endings are the same except for **nosotros** (-emos vs. -imos) and **vosotros** (-éis vs. -ís).

In medicine you will mostly use the **usted** form, the polite "you." It shares the ending of él/ella: "¿Usted **fuma**?" (Do you smoke?), "¿**Toma** medicinas?" (Do you take medicines?).

Because the ending already shows the subject, Spanish often leaves out the pronoun: "**Trabajo** en el hospital" means "I work in the hospital."

A real example from a clinic visit: "¿Dónde **vive** usted? ¿Con quién **vive**?" (Where do you live? Who do you live with?). These questions are part of the social history.
levels.college:
The Spanish **presente de indicativo** is built from stem + person/number ending. Regular verbs keep the stem unchanged across the whole paradigm, so learning the endings opens up hundreds of clinical verbs.

**Endings:**
- -ar: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an
- -er: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en
- -ir: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en

The **theme vowel** sets the pattern: -ar verbs use *a*, while -er and -ir share *e* except in nosotros/vosotros forms.

**High-yield regular verbs for patient care:**
- -ar: tomar (take), fumar (smoke), respirar (breathe), trabajar (work), necesitar (need), usar (use), orinar (urinate), sudar (sweat), vomitar (vomit), cambiar (change)
- -er: toser (cough), beber (drink), comer (eat), comprender (understand)
- -ir: vivir (live), sufrir (suffer), escribir (write), recibir (receive), subir (go up), abrir (open)

**Uses of the present tense in clinic:**
- Habitual actions: "¿Cuántas horas **duerme**?" asks about routine, though dormir is irregular. A regular verb works the same way: "¿**Bebe** alcohol?"
- Ongoing states: "**Sufro** de asma" (I have asthma).
- Near future: "Mañana **recibe** los resultados" (Tomorrow you get the results).
- Duration with **hace...que** or **desde hace**: "**Toso** desde hace tres días" (I've been coughing for three days). English uses the present perfect here, but Spanish uses the simple present.

**Register:** use **usted/ustedes** with patients unless invited to use tú. Usted takes third-person endings: "¿Usted **respira** bien?" Many learners wrongly use the tú form (-as/-es), which can sound overly familiar.

**Questions:** intonation or inversion turns statements into questions: "¿Fuma usted?" / "¿Usted fuma?". Spanish needs no helper verb like English "do."
levels.phd:
Morphologically, a Spanish present-indicative form segments as **root + theme vowel + person/number suffix**: habl-a-mos, com-e-mos, viv-i-mos. In the first-person singular, the theme vowel drops before **-o** (habl-o, not *habl-a-o). The three conjugation classes come from Latin: -ar from the Latin first conjugation (-āre), -er merging the Latin second and third (-ēre, -ere), and -ir from the fourth (-īre). That merger explains why -er and -ir endings are so alike.

**Productivity:** -ar is the only fully productive class. New verbs nearly always enter as -ar, including clinical coinages such as *escanear* (to scan), *intubar* (to intubate), *monitorizar/monitorear* (to monitor) and *suturar* (to suture). So most medical procedure verbs are regular -ar, which makes them easy to conjugate.

**Stress:** in the present tense, regular verbs stress the stem in the singular and third-person plural (res**pi**ro, res**pi**ran), and the ending in nosotros/vosotros (respi**ra**mos). Written accents mark only the vosotros forms (-áis, -éis, -ís). Some -iar/-uar verbs place stress on the i or u and need a written accent: *envío*, *continúo*; *cambiar* does not (*cambio*). These verbs follow the regular endings but show a stress contrast that learners often miss.

**Pronoun omission:** Spanish is a **null-subject (pro-drop)** language. Because the endings mark the subject, overt pronouns add emphasis or contrast. In clinic, though, **usted** is often kept, both for politeness and because *toma* could mean he, she or you.

**Tense semantics:** the Spanish simple present covers ground that English splits between the simple and progressive present. *Respira con dificultad* can mean "breathes with difficulty" as a habit or "is breathing with difficulty" right now. The progressive (*está respirando*) exists but is used less often and stresses that the action is happening at this moment.

**Regional variation:** **vosotros** forms are used mainly in Spain. In Latin America, **ustedes** serves for both formal and informal plural "you." In voseo regions such as Argentina, Uruguay and much of Central America, *vos* has its own endings: *vos hablás, comés, vivís*.
levels.expert:
For clinical fluency, the goal is to produce regular present-tense forms quickly and accurately under pressure, especially in history taking. Some practical points and pitfalls:

**History-taking frames built on regular verbs:**
- Social history: "¿**Fuma** cigarrillos? ¿Desde cuándo **fuma**?" / "¿**Bebe** alcohol? ¿Cuántas veces por semana?" / "¿**Usa** drogas?" Keep these questions neutral and nonjudgmental.
- Medications: "¿Qué medicinas **toma**?" Note that *tomar* covers "take" medicine and also "drink." Context decides the meaning, so a follow-up like "¿**toma** alcohol?" is clear.
- Function: "¿**Camina** sin ayuda?" "¿**Orina** bien?" "¿**Respira** bien cuando **sube** las escaleras?"
- Living situation: "¿**Vive** solo/sola?", which is key for discharge planning after neurosurgery.

**Duration constructions:** "¿Desde cuándo **tose**?" → "**Toso** desde hace una semana" / "Hace una semana que **toso**." English speakers often wrongly use a past form here, which shifts the meaning toward an action that has finished.

**Pitfalls:**
- Person mismatch: *usted habla* vs. *tú hablas*. Switching between forms during one visit sounds careless.
- First-person replies: patients answer in yo forms (*sufro, tomo, vivo*). Recognizing *-o* as "I" helps you track who did what, for example "mi esposo **fuma**, yo no **fumo**."
- False friends: *asistir* means to attend, not to assist (use *ayudar*). *Molestar* means to bother, as in "¿Le molesta la luz?" (Does the light bother you?), not to molest. Misusing it can be alarming.
- Overregularization: under stress, learners apply regular endings to stem-changing verbs, producing *dormo* instead of *duermo* or *sento* instead of *siento*. Learn the regular core first, then add irregular verbs as a separate set.

**Evidence and equity:** language-concordant care and professional interpreters improve comprehension and outcomes for patients with limited English proficiency. Partial fluency carries a risk of errors, so learners should use certified interpreters for consent and complex discussions. Grammatical accuracy in simple frames like these is a foundation, not a replacement for those safeguards.

keyPoints: Spanish infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir; drop the ending to find the stem
-ar endings: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an
-er and -ir share endings except nosotros (-emos/-imos) and vosotros (-éis/-ís)
With patients use usted, which takes the él/ella ending: ¿Usted fuma?
The simple present plus desde hace shows ongoing duration: Toso desde hace tres días
New medical verbs (intubar, escanear) enter as regular -ar verbs

test.q: What is the yo form of tomar?
test.explain: Drop -ar and add -o: tomo. Toma is the usted/él form.

test.q: Which form correctly asks a patient 'Do you smoke?' politely?
test.explain: Usted takes the third-person ending -a. Fumas is the tú form, and fumo means 'I smoke.'

test.q: The nosotros form of vivir is:
test.explain: -ir verbs use -imos for nosotros. -emos belongs to -er verbs.

test.q: In which forms do -er and -ir present endings differ?
test.explain: They differ only in nosotros (-emos/-imos) and vosotros (-éis/-ís).

test.q: How do you say 'I have been coughing for three days'?
test.explain: Spanish uses the simple present with desde hace for actions that are still going on.

test.q: Which verb is a regular -er verb?
test.explain: Toser (to cough) ends in -er. Respirar and orinar are -ar verbs; sufrir is an -ir verb.

test.q: Why can Spanish often leave out subject pronouns?
test.explain: Spanish is pro-drop: the ending already marks the person, so trabajo means 'I work.'

test.q: Which conjugation class do most new medical verbs like intubar join?
test.explain: -ar is the only fully productive class, so new verbs such as escanear and suturar enter as -ar.

test.q: The ellos form of comer is:
test.explain: -er verbs take -en in the third-person plural.

test.q: The basic form of a verb, ending in -ar, -er or -ir, is the ___.
test.explain: Hablar, comer and vivir are infinitives.

test.q: Give the usted form ('you drink') of the regular -er verb meaning 'to drink.'
test.explain: Beber drops -er and adds -e for usted: ¿Bebe alcohol?

test.q: Changing a verb's ending to match its subject is called ___.
test.explain: Conjugation adds person and number endings to the stem.

kidTest.q: What does 'yo como' mean?
kidTest.explain: Comer means to eat, so yo como is 'I eat.'

kidTest.q: Which ending do you add for 'I'?
kidTest.explain: Hablo, como, vivo all end in -o.

kidTest.q: Which word is a verb family ending?
kidTest.explain: The three verb families are -ar, -er and -ir.

kidTest.q: What does 'hablar' mean?
kidTest.explain: Hablar means to talk or speak.

kidTest.q: Fill in 'I live': yo v _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Vivir loses -ir and gets -o: vivo.

advancedTest.q: Why are -er and -ir present endings nearly identical?
choices: Most -ir verbs evolved later out of older -ar verbs
Spanish borrowed its -ir endings from medieval Arabic
The Spanish academy unified both sets in the 1800s
advancedTest.explain: The Latin second and third conjugations merged into -er, while -ir comes from the fourth; their shared inherited patterns leave differences only in nosotros and vosotros.

advancedTest.q: A clinician says 'Tosió desde hace una semana.' What is the main problem?
choices: The pronoun usted is left out
A past form suggests the cough has ended
Toser is an -ir verb in this context
advancedTest.explain: An ongoing duration with desde hace needs the simple present (tose).

advancedTest.q: Why do clinicians often keep 'usted' despite pro-drop grammar?
choices: Patients tend to answer in usted forms themselves
Omitting usted is ungrammatical in formal speech
Usted verbs carry their own distinct set of endings
It clarifies an ambiguous ending and adds courtesy
advancedTest.explain: Toma could mean he, she or you, so usted makes the subject clear and sounds polite. Usted shares the él/ella ending rather than having its own.

advancedTest.q: A tense learner says 'dormo' for 'I sleep.' This error best shows:
choices: Influence from voseo verb forms in Argentina
A false-friend confusion with a similar verb
A misplaced written accent on the stem vowel
advancedTest.explain: The correct form is duermo. Applying regular patterns to stem-changing verbs is overregularization.

lessons.title: Doler and Gustar-Type Verbs: Me duele la cabeza

levels.kid:
In English we say "My head hurts." The head is doing the hurting. Spanish flips it around! Spanish says **Me duele la cabeza**. That means "The head hurts me."

Think of a pain as a little visitor that bothers you. The visitor is the thing that hurts. You are the one who feels it.

- **Me duele la cabeza.** My head hurts.
- **Me duele la panza.** My tummy hurts.
- **Me duelen los pies.** My feet hurt.

See the extra **n** in **duelen**? When two or more things hurt, like two feet, the word gets an n.

A doctor might ask you: **¿Te duele?** That means "Does it hurt you?" You can answer **Sí** or **No**.
levels.hs:
**Doler** means "to hurt" or "to ache." It works like **gustar** ("to please"). In these verbs, the thing that hurts is the grammatical **subject**. The person who feels it is shown by an **indirect object pronoun** placed before the verb.

The pronouns are:
- **me** (me), **te** (you, informal), **le** (him, her, or you formal)
- **nos** (us), **les** (them, or you all)

The verb usually appears in only two forms:
- **duele** when one thing hurts: **Me duele la garganta.** My throat hurts.
- **duelen** when several things hurt: **Me duelen las rodillas.** My knees hurt.

Notice that **doler** is a **stem-changing verb**. The o in the stem becomes ue (d**ue**le). Also notice that Spanish uses **la** (the) with the body part, not "my."

A clinician speaking formally asks: **¿Le duele el pecho?** Does your chest hurt? To ask where, say **¿Dónde le duele?** Where does it hurt?

To add clarity or emphasis, Spanish adds **a + person**: **A mi hijo le duele el oído.** My son's ear hurts. Here **le** stays in the sentence even though "a mi hijo" is also named.

Other verbs built the same way include **gustar**, **molestar** (to bother), and **picar** (to itch).
levels.college:
Gustar-type verbs reverse the English mapping of roles. The experiencer (the person who feels) is the **indirect object** (IO). The stimulus (the body part or thing) is the **subject**, and the verb agrees with it. This is why the verb stays in third person: **me duele**, **me duelen**, never "yo duelo" for "I hurt."

**Structure:** (a + experiencer) + IO pronoun + verb + subject
- **(A mí) me duele la espalda.** My back hurts.
- **(A usted) le duelen los oídos.** Your ears hurt.
- **(A ella) le pica la piel.** Her skin itches.

**Key rules:**
- The IO pronoun is required. **A usted** is optional, but **le** is not. "A usted duele" is ungrammatical.
- **Le** is ambiguous (him, her, you formal). Add **a usted**, **a él**, or **a ella** to make it clear, which is useful in a busy room.
- Doler is **o→ue** stem-changing in the present tense: **duele** and **duelen**. The present subjunctive also changes (duela, duelan), but these forms have no stem change: **dolía** (imperfect, "was hurting"), **dolió** (preterite, "hurt"), **ha dolido**.
- The subject usually follows the verb and takes a definite article. Body-part articles are covered in their own lesson.
- An infinitive used as the subject takes singular agreement: **Me duele tragar.** It hurts to swallow. **¿Le duele respirar hondo?** Does it hurt to breathe deeply?

**Clinically useful relatives:**
- **molestar** (to bother): **Me molesta la luz.** Light bothers me.
- **picar** (to itch, sting): **Me pican los ojos.**
- **arder** (to burn): **Me arde al orinar.** It burns when I urinate.
- **faltar** (to lack): **Me falta el aire.** I'm short of breath.
- **gustar**, **parecer**, **quedar** (**Le quedan tres pastillas.** He has three pills left.)

**Noun alternative:** **el dolor** (pain): **Tengo dolor de cabeza.** Both forms are natural.
levels.phd:
Linguistically, doler belongs to the class of **psych / experiencer-object predicates**, also called *gustar*-class or "reverse" verbs. In these verbs the experiencer is marked with **dative case**, so the clitic is me/te/le/nos/les and never the accusative lo/la. The theme (the stimulus) controls verb agreement. Belletti and Rizzi's (1988) analysis of Italian *piacere*-type verbs is the classic account. The dative experiencer behaves as a syntactic quasi-subject: it is typically **preverbal** and topical, while the nominative theme is **postverbal**. Hence the unmarked order is *A Juan le duele la muela*, not *La muela le duele a Juan*. The second order is grammatical but places contrastive focus on the experiencer.

**Clitic doubling.** In standard Spanish, a full dative phrase (*a Juan*) is almost always doubled by *le*. With experiencer verbs, doubling is effectively obligatory. A frequent learner error is *le* agreement failure: *a mis padres le duele* should be *les duele*. In much colloquial speech across Spain and the Americas, however, singular *le* with a plural referent is widespread, so you will hear patients use it.

**Aspect matters clinically:**
- **Me dolía** (imperfect) means an ongoing or background ache.
- **Me dolió** (preterite) means a bounded episode: *Me dolió cuando me agaché.* It hurt when I bent down.
- **Me ha dolido** is preferred in much of Spain for the recent past. **Me dolió** is preferred across most of Latin America.
- **Me duele desde hace tres días** means it has hurt for three days. Spanish uses the present tense here, where English uses the present perfect.

**Pronominal doler.** **Dolerse de** is a different verb meaning "to complain of" or "to grieve": *se duele del abdomen* in clinical notes. Do not confuse it with the experiencer construction.

The **estar + adolorido/dolorido** construction (*Estoy adolorido*, "I'm sore") offers an adjectival alternative. *Adolorido* is common in Mexico and Central America, and *dolorido* in Spain. Choosing the patient's variant builds rapport.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, the grammar of doler becomes a tool for precise pain assessment. You can build an OPQRST-style history mostly from experiencer-verb frames:

- **Onset:** *¿Desde cuándo le duele?* Since when does it hurt you?
- **Provocation:** *¿Le duele más al caminar / al toser / al acostarse?* Does it hurt more when you walk / cough / lie down?
- **Region and radiation:** *¿Dónde le duele? ¿El dolor se le corre a la pierna?* Where does it hurt? Does the pain shoot into your leg? Note the ethical dative *se le*, which is common in Mexican Spanish and essential for radicular pain. *Se le va / se le baja / se le corre* all mean "it travels."
- **Severity:** *Del 0 al 10, ¿cuánto le duele?* From 0 to 10, how much does it hurt?
- **Timing:** *¿Le duele todo el tiempo o le va y viene?* Does it hurt all the time, or does it come and go?
- **Response to the exam:** *Avíseme si le duele cuando aprieto.* Tell me if it hurts when I press.

**Pitfalls:**
- **Register.** Use *le* with *usted* for adult patients, and *te* only with children or when invited. Mixing *¿Te duele…?* with *usted* commands sounds careless.
- **Ambiguous *le*.** Speaking to a parent about a child, *¿Le duele?* can mean the parent or the child. Say *¿A él le duele?* or *¿A la niña le duele?*
- **Agreement slips.** Mistakes like *Me duele los pies* are a classic error by clinicians, not patients. Patients understand you, but documentation that quotes them should be accurate.
- **Quality words.** Patients describe the quality of pain with descriptors, not with doler: *punzante* (stabbing), *ardoroso* (burning), *opresivo* (pressing), *pulsátil* (throbbing), *como toques* (electric). Ask *¿Cómo es el dolor?* What is the pain like?
- **Cultural idioms.** *Me duele el cerebro* or *me duele el cerebro de atrás* can mean occipital headache, and *me duele el corazón* may be grief rather than angina. Clarify before you anchor.

For neurosurgical work, the frames *me duele / se me duerme / me hormiguea / me falta fuerza* (it hurts / it goes numb / it tingles / I lack strength) together separate pain from numbness, paresthesia and weakness. All four are experiencer constructions, so mastering this one grammatical pattern lets you describe them all.

Research on language-concordant care links clinicians' Spanish proficiency to better patient comprehension and satisfaction. Still, verify your skills and use a certified interpreter for consent or complex discussions.

keyPoints: Doler works like gustar: the body part is the subject
The person who hurts is an indirect object pronoun: me, te, le, nos, les
Use duele for one thing and duelen for plural things
Doler is o→ue stem-changing in the present indicative and subjunctive
A + person clarifies or emphasizes, but the pronoun stays
Molestar, picar, arder and faltar follow the same pattern

lessons.title: Tener Expressions: Tener fiebre, frío, sed y náuseas

levels.kid:
In English we say "I **am** cold" or "I **am** thirsty." In Spanish, people say "I **have** cold" and "I **have** thirst"! The verb **tener** means "to have."

- **Tengo frío.** = I am cold. (I have cold.)
- **Tengo calor.** = I am hot.
- **Tengo sed.** = I am thirsty.
- **Tengo hambre.** = I am hungry.
- **Tengo fiebre.** = I have a fever.

Think of feelings as little backpacks you carry. You can "have" a cold feeling or a thirsty feeling, and later you can put it down.

A doctor might ask a child, "¿Tienes fiebre?" That means "Do you have a fever?" You can answer, "Sí, tengo fiebre," or "No, no tengo fiebre."
levels.hs:
**Tener** (to have) is one of the most useful verbs in medical Spanish because many body feelings are expressed with it. English uses "to be" (I am cold), but Spanish uses "to have" plus a noun (tengo frío, literally "I have cold").

Present tense of tener (it's irregular):
- yo **tengo**
- tú **tienes**
- él / ella / usted **tiene**
- nosotros **tenemos**
- ellos / ellas / ustedes **tienen**

Key expressions for patient care:
- **tener fiebre**: to have a fever
- **tener frío / calor**: to be cold / hot
- **tener sed / hambre**: to be thirsty / hungry
- **tener náuseas**: to be nauseated
- **tener sueño**: to be sleepy
- **tener miedo**: to be afraid
- **tener escalofríos**: to have chills

Because frío, sed and hambre are **nouns**, you make them stronger with **mucho/mucha**, not muy: "Tengo **mucho** frío" (I'm very cold), "Tengo **mucha** sed" (I'm very thirsty, since sed is feminine).

Real example at a clinic:
- Médica: "¿Tiene fiebre?" (Do you have a fever?)
- Paciente: "Sí, y tengo escalofríos y mucha sed." (Yes, and I have chills and I'm very thirsty.)

Notice the doctor uses **usted** (tiene) with an adult patient. That is the polite, formal "you."
levels.college:
Spanish encodes many physiological and emotional states as **possessed nouns** with tener, where English uses "be" + adjective. Mastering these is essential for history-taking because patients will answer in these forms.

**Core clinical tener expressions**
- **tener fiebre**: have a fever; **tener temperatura** is common colloquially for the same idea
- **tener escalofríos**: have chills (plural noun)
- **tener náuseas**: be nauseated; in parts of Latin America you'll also hear **tener asco** for nausea or disgust
- **tener frío / calor**: feel cold / hot (a sensation, not body temperature)
- **tener sed / hambre**: be thirsty / hungry (useful when screening for diabetes: polidipsia, polifagia)
- **tener sueño**: be sleepy; contrast **tener insomnio**
- **tener tos, diarrea, gripe, catarro**: have a cough, diarrhea, flu, a cold
- **tener miedo / vergüenza**: be afraid / embarrassed
- **tener ganas de** + infinitive: feel like doing (tener ganas de vomitar = feel like vomiting)
- **tener que** + infinitive: have to (tiene que tomar agua = you have to drink water)

**Intensifiers agree with the noun.** Since these are nouns, use **mucho/mucha/muchos/muchas**: mucho frío, mucha sed, mucha hambre (hambre is feminine, despite taking "el" in the singular), muchas náuseas, muchos escalofríos.

**Frío: tener vs. estar vs. hacer**
- Tengo frío: *I* feel cold.
- Estoy frío: I'm cold to the touch (rare, sometimes odd or even suggestive of a cold body).
- Hace frío: the weather is cold.

**Questions and duration.** Ask with usted: "¿Tiene náuseas?" For onset, combine with hace: "¿Desde cuándo tiene fiebre?" (Since when have you had a fever?) → "Tengo fiebre desde el lunes" or "Hace tres días que tengo fiebre." Spanish uses the **present** tense here where English uses the present perfect ("I have had").
levels.phd:
From a linguistic standpoint, tener expressions are **light-verb constructions**: tener carries little semantic weight and the predicative noun (frío, sed, fiebre) supplies the meaning. This pattern, inherited from Latin *habere* constructions and shared with French (avoir froid, avoir faim) and Italian (avere fame), frames bodily states as possessed entities rather than properties of the subject. English speakers' "be + adjective" mapping is the main source of interference errors such as *"estoy sed"* or *"soy frío"*.

**Grammatical consequences of nounhood**
- Quantification uses **mucho** (determiner agreeing in gender/number), not the adverb muy: *tengo muy frío* is a classic learner error, though "muy" is heard colloquially in some dialects. Hambre is feminine (mucha hambre) but takes el in the singular because of the stressed initial /a/ rule (el hambre, el agua).
- Graded questions can use **cuánto/cuánta**: "¿Cuánta sed tiene?"
- Negation is simple: "No tengo náuseas." No article is needed with mass or abstract nouns: tener fiebre, not *tener una fiebre* (though "una fiebre muy alta" is acceptable when modified).

**Aspect and time**
- Present for ongoing states with duration: "Hace dos días que tengo náuseas."
- Preterite **tuve** marks a bounded episode: "Anoche tuve fiebre" (Last night I had a fever, now gone).
- Imperfect **tenía** describes background or repeated states: "Tenía escalofríos cada noche."
These distinctions matter clinically: tuve vs. tenía can signal a single spike versus a recurring pattern.

**Semantic nuance**
- **Tener calor** reports thermal sensation; **tener fiebre** implies an elevated temperature (often patient-perceived, not measured). **Sentirse afiebrado/a** means feeling feverish.
- **Tener náuseas** vs. **tener ganas de vomitar**: the latter describes impending emesis, the former a broader queasy state; patients may also say "tengo el estómago revuelto" (upset stomach).
- **Tener asco** spans nausea and disgust, so it can be ambiguous.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, tener expressions are where fluent-sounding clinicians most often lose precision. Practical points:

**Verify measured vs. felt fever.** "Tengo fiebre" frequently means "I feel hot" rather than a thermometer reading. Follow up: "¿Se tomó la temperatura? ¿Cuánto marcó el termómetro?" Many patients also say "tengo calentura," a common term in Mexico and Central America; recognize it as fever. **Escalofríos** (chills) is distinct from **temblores** (tremors or shaking) and from **rigidez** (stiffness), and a rigor-type history ("temblaba sin poder controlarlo") deserves its own question.

**Regional and register variants to recognize**
- **Tener mareo / estar mareado**: dizziness, but also motion sickness or nausea in some speakers; always clarify ("¿Siente que todo da vueltas?" for vertigo).
- **Tener basca(s)**: rural or older usage for nausea in parts of Mexico and Spain.
- **Tener el estómago revuelto, tener agruras**: upset stomach, heartburn.
- **Tener susto**: in some Latin American communities, a culturally recognized illness concept, not just "to be scared." Explore it respectfully rather than translating it away.

**Formality and person.** Use **usted** forms (tiene, tenía) with adults unless invited otherwise; with children, **tú** (¿Tienes frío?). For caregivers reporting on a child: "¿El niño tiene fiebre?" Shifting persons mid-interview causes confusion, so name the subject.

**High-yield screening phrases**
- "¿Tiene mucha sed o mucha hambre últimamente?" (hyperglycemia symptoms)
- "¿Tiene náuseas o ganas de vomitar?" (both forms, to catch different idiolects)
- "¿Tiene miedo de algo en su casa?" (safety screening, asked privately)
- "¿Tiene sueño durante el día?" (somnolence; in neurosurgical follow-up, new sleepiness after head injury is a red flag to escalate)

**Pitfalls**
- Saying *"estoy embarazada"* for embarrassed (it means pregnant); embarrassed is **tener vergüenza** or **me da vergüenza**.
- *"Tengo caliente"* is wrong; caliente is an adjective and can carry sexual overtones. Use **tengo calor**.
- **Tener que** creates obligations; in instructions, "tiene que" can sound commanding, so softer "es importante que..." may be kinder.

When precision matters for consent or complex symptoms, use a qualified interpreter.

keyPoints: Spanish uses tener + noun where English uses 'to be': tengo frío = I am cold
Tener is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen
Core clinical set: fiebre, escalofríos, náuseas, frío, calor, sed, hambre, sueño, miedo
Intensify with mucho/mucha, not muy: mucha sed, mucho frío
Duration uses the present: Hace tres días que tengo fiebre
Avoid traps: tengo calor (not tengo caliente), tener vergüenza (not embarazada)

lessons.title: Articles with Body Parts: Why It's Me duele el brazo, Not Mi brazo

levels.kid:
In English we say "my arm hurts." In Spanish, people usually say **el brazo**, which means "the arm," instead of **mi brazo**, "my arm."

Why? Another little word already tells whose arm it is. In **Me duele el brazo** ("my arm hurts"), the word **me** means "to me." So everyone knows it is your arm! Saying "my" again would be like wearing two name tags.

More examples:
- **Me duele la cabeza.** My head hurts.
- **Me lavo las manos.** I wash my hands.
- **Abra la boca.** Open your mouth.

So in Spanish, body parts usually get **el** or **la**, which both mean "the."
levels.hs:
English uses **possessive adjectives** (my, your, his) with body parts: "My stomach hurts." Spanish usually uses the **definite article** instead: **el, la, los, las** ("the").

The reason: the sentence already shows who owns the body part, so "my" is unnecessary. Ownership is usually shown by:
- An **indirect object pronoun** (me, te, le, nos, les): **Me duele el estómago.** My stomach hurts. Here, me points to the owner.
- A **reflexive pronoun** in reflexive verbs: **Me rompí la pierna.** I broke my leg. **Se lava las manos.** She washes her hands.
- The **subject** itself, when the body part obviously belongs to them: **Levante el brazo.** Raise your arm. **Abra los ojos.** Open your eyes.

Saying *Me duele mi brazo* is understandable, but it sounds redundant and non-native, like "to me hurts my arm." A Spanish speaker hears "my" twice.

Real example: a patient in clinic says, **"Doctor, me duele la rodilla derecha."** That means "Doctor, my right knee hurts." No **mi** is needed, because **me** already tells you whose knee it is.

Tip: the article must match the noun's gender and number. Say **la mano** (feminine, despite ending in -o), **el pie**, **los dedos**, **las uñas**.
levels.college:
Spanish treats body parts as **inalienable possession**: things that obviously belong to their owner. Because of this, grammar marks the owner on the verb or pronoun, not with a possessive adjective. The noun usually takes the **definite article**.

**Ways the owner is marked:**
- **Indirect object pronoun** (dative): *Le duele la espalda.* His/her back hurts. *Le voy a examinar el oído.* I'm going to examine your ear.
- **Reflexive pronoun**: *¿Se cortó el dedo?* Did you cut your finger? *Me torcí el tobillo.* I twisted my ankle.
- **Subject control** with obvious ownership: *Cierre los ojos. Doble las rodillas.* Close your eyes. Bend your knees.

**Number agreement.** With plural owners, Spanish usually keeps the body part singular if each person has one: *Abran la boca* (all of you, open your mouths). *Se quitaron el sombrero* is the classic non-body example.

**When the possessive IS used:**
- When ownership would otherwise be unclear or contrastive: *Su brazo está más hinchado que el mío.* Your arm is more swollen than mine.
- When the body part is the **subject** of a sentence with no pronoun pointing to the owner, especially in descriptions: *Mi presión está alta* is common. Speakers also say *Tengo la presión alta*.
- When a modifier makes the part non-obvious or emphasized: *Me duele mi pierna mala* (colloquial).

**Gender traps** relevant to clinic:
- *la mano*, *el día*: exceptions to the -o/-a pattern
- *el agua* but *las aguas*: masculine article before stressed a-
- *el pie / los pies*, *la nariz*, *la piel*, *el corazón*

**Tener with body parts**: *Tengo el tobillo hinchado* (my ankle is swollen) also uses the article plus an adjective.
levels.phd:
The pattern is a textbook case of the **external possessor** or "possessor dative" construction, found across Romance and many European languages (French *Il s'est cassé la jambe*, German *Ich wasche mir die Hände*). English is typologically unusual in requiring possessive determiners with body parts. Haspelmath's work on European external possession treats this as an areal feature of "Standard Average European." Analyses differ on details. The core generalization is this: when a clitic (dative or reflexive) or the subject binds the possessor, the possessum surfaces with a definite article. The article's referent is then fixed by **inalienability**.

**Syntactic facts:**
- The possessor clitic is an **affected** argument, so the construction is felicitous mainly when the possessor experiences the event. *Le examiné la garganta* implies the patient is involved. *Examiné su garganta* is grammatical, but it sounds detached, like reporting on a specimen.
- *Doler* takes a dative experiencer and a nominative theme: *[me]DAT duele [la cabeza]NOM*. Adding *mi* duplicates the possessor. Prescriptive grammars (RAE, *Nueva gramática*, §18) call this redundant except under contrast.
- **Distributive singular**: *Les dolía la cabeza* (each one's head). The plural *las cabezas* is possible but marked.

**Semantic extension.** The article+clitic pattern extends beyond strict body parts to clothing and close personal items: *Quítese la camisa*, *Me robaron la cartera*. It also covers physiological values: *¿Cómo tiene la presión / el azúcar?*

**Regional variation.** Possessive use with body parts is somewhat more frequent in some Latin American varieties and in contact varieties, including U.S. Spanish under English influence: *Me duele mi espalda*. Clinicians should recognize this as a natural variant, not an error to correct. Sociolinguistic work on U.S. heritage speakers documents increased possessive determiner use as a contact effect.

**Possessive *su* ambiguity.** *Su brazo* can mean his, her, your (usted) or their arm. The clitic construction disambiguates through context and the clitic's person, which is one functional rationale for the article pattern.
levels.expert:
For clinicians, mastering this construction does more than make speech sound native. It improves clarity, rapport and safety in the encounter.

**Commands during the exam** (formal usted): *Abra la boca. Saque la lengua. Apriete mi mano.* In the last one, *mi* is correct because the hand is mine, not the patient's. Likewise *Siga mi dedo con los ojos*: the finger is the examiner's, and the eyes take the article. This contrast is a high-yield neuro-exam pattern.

**Clitic plus article for procedures:** *Le voy a tomar la presión. Le voy a revisar los reflejos. Le vamos a poner un suero en el brazo.* The dative *le* signals the action is done to the patient. It sounds warmer and more natural than *Voy a revisar sus reflejos*.

**Pitfalls:**
- **Laterality**: articles do not specify side. Always add *derecho/a* or *izquierdo/a*, agreeing in gender: *el ojo derecho*, *la pierna izquierda*. For wrong-site prevention, have the patient point to the site and confirm verbally.
- ***Le* ambiguity**: *Le duele* can mean you, he or she. When interviewing a family member about a child, clarify: *¿A él le duele el oído?*
- **Leísmo** (Spain): *le* used as a direct object for people is accepted in Peninsular speech. Don't misread *le vi* as an error.
- **Ownership in surrogate history**: *¿Le duele la cabeza a su hijo?* uses clitic doubling with *a + noun* to name the owner explicitly.

**Documentation.** Spanish charts and consent forms use the article pattern in impersonal register: *Se observa edema en el miembro inferior derecho* (right lower limb). Translators converting English notes literally (*su pierna*) produce stilted text, and with *su* they may leave ownership ambiguous.

**Comprehension.** Expect patients, especially in U.S. bilingual settings, to say *mi espalda* or *mi estómago*. Accept these. Correcting a patient's grammar damages rapport.

**Open questions.** It is unclear how these constructions affect comprehension of translated discharge instructions among patients with limited literacy. Whether clinician fluency in such markers measurably improves outcomes is plausible but understudied.

keyPoints: Spanish usually uses el/la/los/las, not mi/tu/su, with body parts
A pronoun (me, te, le, se) or the subject already shows the owner
Me duele el brazo = my arm hurts; me duele mi brazo sounds redundant
Use the possessive for contrast or unclear ownership: su brazo y el mío
Exam contrast: Apriete mi mano (the clinician's hand), Abra la boca (the patient's)
Watch gender (la mano) and add derecho/izquierdo for laterality

test.q: Which is the most natural way to say "My head hurts"?
test.explain: Me already shows the owner, so the definite article la is used. Mi would repeat the owner.

test.q: In "Me rompí la pierna," what shows whose leg it is?
test.explain: The reflexive pronoun me marks the speaker as the owner and the affected person.

test.q: How do you tell a patient "Open your mouth" (usted)?
test.explain: In formal commands, the subject is the obvious owner, so the article la is used.

test.q: Why is "Apriete mi mano" correct during an exam?
choices: The hand belongs to the examiner
Mi refers to the patient here
test.explain: The patient squeezes the clinician's hand, so mi correctly marks a different owner.

test.q: When is a possessive like su natural with a body part?
choices: In any question to a patient
test.explain: Possessives are used for contrast or unclear ownership, as in Su brazo está más hinchado que el mío.

test.q: Which article goes with mano?
test.explain: Mano is feminine despite ending in -o: la mano.

test.q: "Le voy a examinar el oído" means:
choices: I am going to examine your ear.
I examine his ear each morning.
You are going to examine my ear.
test.explain: Le marks the patient as owner and affected person. Voy a examinar is the near future, "I am going to examine."

test.q: Which phrase correctly specifies the left leg?
test.explain: Pierna is feminine, so both the article and the adjective take feminine forms.

test.q: A U.S. patient says "Me duele mi espalda." The best response is to:
test.explain: This is a common, natural variant, especially in contact Spanish. Correcting it harms rapport.

test.q: Spanish usually uses the definite ___, not a possessive, with body parts.
test.explain: El, la, los and las replace mi, tu and su because a pronoun or the subject already marks the owner.

test.q: Translate into Spanish: "I wash my hands." (reflexive)
test.explain: The reflexive me marks the owner, and manos takes las.

test.q: Siga mi dedo con los ___. (Follow my finger with your eyes.)
test.explain: The patient's eyes take the article los, while the examiner's finger takes mi.

kidTest.q: How do you say "my arm hurts" in Spanish?
kidTest.explain: Spanish says "the arm," because me already tells whose arm it is.

kidTest.q: What does "el" mean?
kidTest.explain: El and la both mean "the."

kidTest.q: In "Me duele la cabeza," which word tells it is your head?
kidTest.explain: Me means "to me," so it shows the head is yours.

kidTest.q: "Abra la boca" means:
kidTest.explain: Abra means open, and boca means mouth.

kidTest.q: Fill in: Me lavo las ___ (hands). Hint: m _ _ _ s
kidTest.explain: Manos means hands.

advancedTest.q: Why does "Le examiné la garganta" sound warmer than "Examiné su garganta"?
choices: The dative clitic marks the patient as an affected participant
The preterite tense requires a clitic for body parts
Garganta takes a masculine article after a dative clitic
Su is ungrammatical with feminine nouns in Spanish
advancedTest.explain: The external possessor dative presents the patient as experiencing the event. The possessive version sounds detached, like reporting on a specimen.

advancedTest.q: "Les dolía la cabeza" with a singular noun best illustrates:
choices: Clitic doubling with an explicit a + noun phrase
The distributive singular for one part per person
A gender agreement error that is common in speech
Leísmo as it is used in Peninsular Spanish
advancedTest.explain: When each owner has one such part, Spanish keeps the noun singular. The plural las cabezas is possible but marked.

advancedTest.q: Interviewing a mother about her son, why say "¿A él le duele el oído?"
choices: Doler takes a direct object when the owner is male
Oído switches to a masculine article after a él
Le alone could mean you, he or she
Él replaces the need for a definite article
advancedTest.explain: Le is ambiguous across usted, él and ella. Clitic doubling with a él names the owner explicitly.

advancedTest.q: English is described as typologically unusual in this domain because it:
choices: Marks body-part owners through dative pronouns
Uses reflexive verbs for actions on the body
Requires possessive determiners with body parts
Lacks any form of definite article before nouns
advancedTest.explain: Many European languages use external possessors plus an article. English instead obligatorily says "my arm."
